opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's actually right there in the name. A PhD is a "Doctor of Philosophy," and people tend to forget that. Whether you're in computer vision, chemistry, or economics, the degree was originally about training you to think deeply about the nature of knowledge in your field, not just to produce papers.

When I was doing my PhD, a lot of the day-to-day was very engineering-heavy: running experiments, tuning models, chasing deadlines. It's easy to get lost in that and become a sort of very skilled technician. What I gradually realized is that the most important questions in research are often philosophical ones. What does it mean for a machine to "see"? What is a representation? Is intelligence something you build from the bottom up, or something that emerges from the right objective and enough data? Those aren't purely technical questions. They're questions about epistemology, about the mind, about what understanding even is.

So reading philosophy, for me, isn't something separate from research. It gives you a different vocabulary and a longer time horizon. Philosophers have been arguing about perception, language, and knowledge for thousands of years, and many of the debates we have in AI today, like whether language alone is enough for intelligence or whether you need grounding in the physical world, have echoes in very old arguments. Reading that work helps you avoid reinventing the wheel, and sometimes it helps you notice when the whole field is asking the wrong question.

I'd also say there's a personal side. A PhD is long, lonely, and full of failure. Philosophy helps you reflect on why you're doing what you're doing, what counts as a meaningful contribution, and how to keep your own taste instead of just following trends. In a field moving as fast as AI, that kind of grounding is maybe more valuable than ever.

So I see them as closely connected. The PhD gives you the tools, and philosophy helps you decide what's worth using them on.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a nice question, because I actually think they're much closer than people assume. "PhD" literally means Doctor of Philosophy, and most of us forget that. We treat it as a technical credential: you learn to train models, write papers, get them accepted. But the original idea was that you're being trained to think, to ask what a question even means before you try to answer it.

When I was a student I didn't read much philosophy at all. I was very focused on the engineering side, getting things to work on ImageNet and so on. It was later, when I started advising students and running a lab, that I felt I needed it. Because the hardest part of research is not solving the problem, it's choosing the problem. And that's a philosophical act. Why do we believe scaling is the answer? What do we mean when we say a model "understands" an image? What counts as evidence? Philosophy doesn't give you the answers, but it gives you a vocabulary and a kind of discipline for noticing your own assumptions.

I'd say the second thing it does is help with taste. In a field moving this fast, there's enormous pressure to follow whatever is trending. Reading people like Kuhn or even older thinkers reminds you that fields go through paradigms, that today's consensus is temporary, and that the interesting work often sits at the edges where the current framework is uncomfortable. That gives you some courage to work on things that aren't fashionable yet.

So I don't think every PhD student needs to take a philosophy course. But I'd encourage them to read a little, especially about epistemology and the history of science. It makes you a better scientist, and honestly it makes the frustrating years of a PhD more meaningful, because you understand what you're actually doing is participating in a very old project of figuring out how we know things.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is learning how to ask questions. A PhD gives you training in a particular field: you learn its methods, what counts as evidence, and how to make progress on a problem. But you can become so focused on solving the problem that you stop asking why it’s framed that way in the first place.

Philosophy encourages you to step back. What assumptions are we making? What do we mean by knowledge or understanding? In AI, those questions are quite close to the technical work, even if an experiment can’t settle them entirely.

So I see them as complementary. Research pushes you to make a question precise enough to test; philosophy can help you notice what that precision leaves out. You don’t need a PhD to read philosophy, of course. But ideally, both make you more comfortable questioning what you think you know.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they can complement each other. A PhD trains you to go very deep into a narrow question: define the problem, choose a method, and produce evidence. Reading philosophy can make you step back and ask, “Why is this the right question? What assumptions am I making? What would count as an answer?”

That’s especially useful in AI, where we use words like intelligence, understanding, and reasoning all the time. We can measure something very precisely without being equally precise about what it means.

But I wouldn’t equate having a PhD with being philosophical. You can be an excellent researcher without reading much philosophy, and you certainly don’t need a PhD to think deeply. For me, the connection is the willingness to examine your assumptions—including the assumptions that have made you successful.
